claims.claim: Anthropic's Opus 5.5 launch post states: "Our tests show that at default settings it will cost 40% less than Opus 5 on typical workloads."
Claude Opus 5.5 lists at $4/MTok input and $20/MTok output, versus Opus 5's $5 and $25 — a 20% cut on both.
Opus 5.5 cache reads cost $0.20/MTok versus Opus 5's $0.50 — a 60% cut, achieved by a model-specific 0.05x multiplier on base input price instead of the standard 0.1x.
Claude Opus 5.5's API default effort is `medium`, while Claude Opus 5 and earlier Opus models default to `high`, so a request omitting `effort` runs one level lower than it did on Opus 5.
Artificial Analysis measured Opus 5.5 at max effort at $5.98 per Intelligence Index task versus Opus 5 at max at $5.86 — cost roughly flat, up 2.0%.
Artificial Analysis measured Opus 5 at high effort (its default) at $3.61 per Intelligence Index task, index score 48, 81M output tokens, $4,331.68 to run the full index.
Artificial Analysis publishes an Opus 5.5 cost-per-task ladder of $0.55 (low), $1.34 (medium), $1.82 (high), $3.46 (xhigh), $5.98 (max), with index scores 42, 51, 54, 56, 58.
Comparing each model at its own default effort on Artificial Analysis data, Opus 5.5 medium ($1.34) versus Opus 5 high ($3.61) is a 62.9% cost reduction — more than Anthropic's 40% claim.
assumptions: Both figures are Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3.2 cost-per-task measurements, so they share a workload and a pricing method.
Medium is treated as Opus 5.5's API default and high as Opus 5's, per Anthropic's effort documentation.
List prices are used throughout; no negotiated or committed-spend discount is modelled.

claims.claim: Cursor's public CursorBench 4.0 leaderboard lists Opus 5.5 Max at 57.8% and $13.43 per task versus Opus 5 Max at 46.6% and $11.95 per task.
At the Max effort setting Cursor's own tweet cites for its 57.8% score, Cursor's published leaderboard shows Opus 5.5 costing 12.4% more per task than Opus 5, not 40% less.
assumptions: Both figures are CursorBench 4.0 average-cost-per-task rows measured at Max effort on the same task set.
Cursor computes cost by applying each model's published per-million-token pricing across input, cache read, cache write and output, so the two rows are priced on the same basis.
Cursor's own variance disclaimer applies; the underlying task count and trials per task are unpublished.

claims.claim: Cursor's CursorBench leaderboard states cost per task is computed by applying each model's published per-million-token pricing across input, cache read, cache write and output to the tokens used on each task.
Cursor's own model documentation claims only that Opus 5.5 "costs 20% less than Opus 5 per token" — the 40% per-task figure appears only in its launch-day X post.
Anthropic's own cost-engineering blog post prices an identical session on both models holding token counts fixed and finds it "costs about 31% less" — a price-only effect, not 40%.

Anthropic's cost blog states a 2.8M-input-token task costs $11.20 uncached, $1.62 at a 90% cache hit rate and about $0.99 at 96%, and that on Opus 5.5 a cached read costs 5% of a fresh input token while an output token costs 100 times a cache read.
Artificial Analysis measured Opus 5.5 at max effort emitting about 119k output tokens per task versus Opus 5's 73k — roughly 1.6x — and 260M versus 140M output tokens across the full index.
Anthropic's docs state that at the same effort setting Opus 5.5 tends to think more per turn than Opus 5, most of all at xhigh and max.

Lovable published a matched-effort comparison at low, medium and high showing Opus 5.5 using 26-57% fewer steps per task and 21-59% fewer input tokens, with every difference significant at the 95% level.

Lovable measured output tokens falling 37-64% on iterative code fixing and verification but staying close to Opus 5's on 0-to-1 app building, indicating savings come from fewer search and verify loops rather than terser writing.
SonarSource measured output tokens falling 40% from 21.71M to 12.96M across 4,444 Java coding tasks, with pass rate slightly down from 88.6% to 87.68%.

Anthropic states Opus 5.5 was evaluated with production safeguards enabled, that intervening safeguards routed cybersecurity tasks to Opus 4.8 and biology and frontier-LLM tasks to Opus 5, and that this likely reduces Opus 5.5's measured benchmark performance.

Anthropic's refusals-and-fallback documentation defines five refusal categories (cyber, bio, frontier_llm, reasoning_extraction, general_harms) and states the routing is applied server-side and is not published per model on the Models API.

Vals AI ran Opus 5.5 with Opus 5 and Opus 4.8 as server-side fallbacks and reported that scoring fallback-assisted tasks as failures moves SRE Bench from 33.59% to 5.34%, with 217 of 262 tasks fallback-assisted.

Anthropic's docs state that changing top-level effort between requests invalidates the prompt cache, and that a per-message effort change preserves it on Opus 5.5, Opus 5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 under a beta header.

The Anthropic Messages API returns input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_creation_input_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens and output_tokens_details.thinking_tokens, with total input equal to cache reads plus cache creation plus input_tokens, making a cost comparison independently auditable.
Anthropic's docs state billed output tokens do not match visible token counts because callers are billed for the full thinking process, not the visible thinking content.
Epoch AI measured the cost of a fixed level of AI performance falling an average of about 47% per quarter, roughly 13x per year, across five benchmarks since 2023.
Epoch AI found cost falls 66% per quarter for performance that has just debuted as state of the art, and 32% per quarter two years later.
Anthropic's Opus-line list price history is $15/$75 at Claude 3 Opus in March 2024, unchanged through Opus 4.1, $5/$25 from Opus 4.5 in November 2025 through Opus 5, and $4/$20 at Opus 5.5.
Anthropic's pricing docs state that Claude 4.7 and later models use a newer tokenizer that produces approximately 30% more tokens for the same text.

Anthropic ran the same rhetorical structure at Opus 4.5 in November 2025, pairing a token-price cut with a claim that at medium effort the model matched Sonnet 4.5's best SWE-bench Verified score using 76% fewer output tokens.

Claude Code version 2.1.280 added Opus 5.5 and changed the default model on Pro and Team Standard plans from Sonnet to Opus, and a stored /effort level no longer carries over to newly released models.

Anthropic's pricing docs state that specifying US-only inference through the inference_geo parameter incurs a 1.1x multiplier on all token pricing categories, and that regional and multi-region endpoints carry a 10% premium over global endpoints.
Anthropic's launch page states that unless otherwise noted all Claude Opus 5.5 benchmark results use adaptive thinking at max effort, while the 40% cost claim is scoped to default settings.
ARC Prize measured Opus 5.5 scoring non-monotonically across effort on ARC-AGI-2, peaking at high effort (93.3%) rather than max (91.7%).
GPT-6 Sol was published at $2/MTok input and $10/MTok output with $0.20 cached input roughly 100 minutes after Anthropic's Opus 5.5 announcement on 2026-09-22.
Anthropic's cost blog states cache-dominated sessions save up to 60% on input while short prompts with long answers save up to 20%.
